introduction: The review aimed to evaluate the effects of structured exercise on depressive symptoms, anxiety and HRQoL in adults with rheumatoid arthritis, and, where data allowed, whether effects differed between conventional and mind-body exercise. The authors state that whether exercise improves these outcomes remains uncertain.
methodology: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials comparing structured exercise with non-exercise control conditions, in adults aged 18 years or older with RA. PubMed, Embase, CENTRAL, Web of Science, Scopus, PsycINFO, and EBSCOhost were searched from inception to November 26, 2025, and two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts. Random-effects meta-analyses in RevMan 5.4 used Hedges’ g; risk of bias was assessed with RoB 2 and certainty with GRADE.
theory: The review was conducted and reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement; no theory is named as guiding the review.
results: Depressive symptoms (11 trials, 685 participants): SMD = −0.49; 95% CI, −0.70 to −0.28; P < 0.001; I² = 42%. Anxiety (7 trials, 403 participants): SMD = −0.45; 95% CI, −0.65 to −0.25; P < 0.001; I² = 0%. Quality of life (7 trials, 564 participants): SMD = 0.45; 95% CI, 0.18 to 0.71; P = 0.001; I² = 50%. No statistically significant subgroup difference between conventional and mind-body exercise was observed for these outcomes. Certainty was rated moderate for depressive symptoms and low for anxiety and HRQoL.
discussion: The authors conclude that structured exercise was associated with reductions in depressive symptoms and anxiety and with improvements in HRQoL, and that exercise may provide psychological and quality-of-life benefits as an adjunct to standard RA care. They state that current evidence is insufficient to identify the most effective exercise modality, dose, supervision strategy, or delivery format, and that exercise should not be viewed as a substitute for pharmacologic disease control or formal mental-health care when these are indicated.
limitations: The authors note that the included trials were generally small and varied in intervention characteristics, comparator conditions, and outcome instruments, and that most psychological and HRQoL outcomes were self-reported with participant blinding usually infeasible. Few studies per outcome limited subgroup precision and the assessment of publication bias. Most analyses used immediate post-intervention outcomes, so durability remains uncertain. The review included only English-language full-text articles, which the authors say may have introduced language bias.

introduction.q: Accordingly, this systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the effects of structured exercise interventions on depressive symptoms, anxiety, and HRQoL in adults with RA.
Where sufficient data were available, we further examined whether these effects differed between conventional exercise and mind-body exercise interventions.
However, whether exercise interventions improve depressive symptoms, anxiety, and HRQoL in adults with RA remains uncertain.

discussion.q: structured exercise interventions were associated with reductions in depressive symptoms and anxiety and with improvements in health-related quality of life (HRQoL) among adults with rheumatoid arthritis (RA)
These findings suggest that exercise may provide psychological and quality-of-life benefits as an adjunct to standard RA care.
However, current evidence is insufficient to identify the most effective exercise modality, dose, supervision strategy, or delivery format.
Exercise should not be viewed as a substitute for pharmacologic disease control or formal mental-health care when these are indicated.

limitations.q: The included trials were generally small and varied substantially in intervention characteristics, comparator conditions, and outcome instruments.
Most psychological and HRQoL outcomes were self-reported, and participant blinding was usually infeasible
reducing the precision of subgroup analyses and limiting the ability to assess publication bias, particularly for anxiety and HRQoL.
Most analyses used immediate post-intervention outcomes because long-term follow-up data were limited; therefore, the durability of benefit remains uncertain.
This restriction may have introduced language bias and is acknowledged as a limitation.

abstract_claims.q: Although exercise is recommended as part of comprehensive care, its effects on psychological outcomes and quality of life remain uncertain.

Compared with non-exercise controls, structured exercise reduced depressive symptoms (11 trials, 685 participants; standardized mean difference, −0.49; 95% confidence interval, −0.70 to −0.28; P < 0.001; I² = 42%; moderate certainty).

Low-certainty evidence suggested reductions in anxiety (7 trials, 403 participants; standardized mean difference, −0.45; 95% confidence interval, −0.65 to −0.25; P < 0.001; I² = 0%) and improvements in quality of life or health-related quality of life (7 trials, 564 participants; Hedges’ g standardized mean difference, 0.45; 95% confidence interval, 0.18 to 0.71; P = 0.001; I² = 50%).
Subgroup analyses showed no statistically significant difference between conventional exercise and mind-body exercise.

Structured exercise probably reduces depressive symptoms and may reduce anxiety and improve quality of life in adults with rheumatoid arthritis, supporting its use as an adjunct to comprehensive care.
Larger, better-reported trials with longer follow-up are needed to clarify durability, clinical importance, and optimal delivery.

caveats.q: Only articles published in English were eligible for inclusion.
Grey literature sources were not systematically searched.

caveats.q: Meta-regression was not conducted because the number of studies per outcome was insufficient and relevant covariates were inconsistently reported.
Formal tests for funnel plot asymmetry were not performed because the number of studies remained small
Several trials were small, with six trials enrolling fewer than 60 participants in total, which should be considered when interpreting the precision and robustness of the pooled estimates.
The included trials were clinically heterogeneous in population characteristics, exercise modality, intervention dose, delivery setting, supervision, and comparator type.
Because exercise interventions are behavioral in nature, blinding of participants and intervention personnel was generally infeasible.
depressive symptoms, anxiety, and HRQoL were mainly assessed using self-reported questionnaires, which may have increased the risk of expectancy or response bias.
In several studies, reporting detail was insufficient to fully judge allocation procedures or prespecification of outcomes.
Missing outcome data were not consistently reported across all trials
Depression outcomes were measured using different instruments, and minimally important change thresholds were not consistently reported in the primary trials.
Statistical heterogeneity was moderate (I² = 42%).
No statistically significant subgroup difference was observed between conventional exercise and mind-body exercise for anxiety (Chi² = 1.29; P = 0.26)
The number of studies contributing to each meta-analysis was modest.

Although the pooled effects were generally favorable, their clinical interpretation depends on the measurement instruments used
but they are less intuitive for clinical decision-making.

Although back-translation and minimal clinically important difference or minimally important difference thresholds can aid clinical interpretation, such interpretation was limited in this review because thresholds vary by instrument, population, baseline severity, and anchor method
Moreover, most trials did not report the proportion of participants achieving clinically meaningful improvement.

Therefore, although the results support the potential benefits of exercise interventions, the extent to which these changes translate into patient-perceived clinical improvement requires further investigation.
The absence of statistically significant subgroup differences between conventional and mind-body exercise should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalence.
These findings support flexibility in exercise selection but do not establish that all exercise formats are interchangeable.
Several plausible mechanisms may explain the observed benefits.
However, mechanistic variables were rarely measured directly in the included trials.
These explanations should therefore be regarded as hypotheses rather than confirmed causal pathways.

Incomplete reporting of participant flow, adverse events, arm-level outcome data, and predefined or protocol-specified outcomes in the primary trials also limited verification and quantitative synthesis for some outcomes.
The evidence is promising but not definitive.
Current evidence does not establish the superiority of any specific exercise modality or delivery format.
